title: Precision without participation: why precision psychiatry needs Collaborative/Therapeutic Assessment.
authors: Aschieri F, Sun Q, Finn SE
abstract:

(2)Central China Normal University, Wuhan, China.

Contemporary psychiatry often assumes that more precise diagnosis will yield 
more effective care. Biomarkers, digital phenotyping, artificial intelligence 
and related tools promise better diagnosis, treatment selection and outcomes. 
Yet this expectation is clinically incomplete: objectively valid information may 
not improve treatment when patients experience it as impersonal, imposed or 
disconnected from their concerns. Collaborative/Therapeutic Assessment (C/TA) 
complements precision psychiatry by engaging patients as partners in 
meaning-making rather than passive recipients o…
reviewer_a_summary: This paper discusses the limitations of precision psychiatry, emphasizing the need for Collaborative/Therapeutic Assessment (C/TA) to enhance patient engagement and treatment effectiveness. While it touches on the use of biomarkers and artificial intelligence in clinical settings, the focus is primarily on psychiatric applications rather than the specific domains of medical AI or computational pathology relevant to the researcher. The paper lacks rigorous external validation or methodological contributions that would be applicable to whole-slide image analysis or survival modeling in oncology. Overall, it does not align with the researcher's interests in pediatric oncology or histopathological analysis.
reviewer_a_comment: The paper is tangentially related to the use of AI in clinical settings but does not address the researcher's specific focus on histopathology, tumor analysis, or pediatric oncology. It fails to provide clinically interpretable outputs or novel methods that could be applied to the researcher's work.
reviewer_b_summary: This paper discusses the limitations of precision psychiatry, emphasizing the need for Collaborative/Therapeutic Assessment (C/TA) to engage patients in their treatment process. It critiques the reliance on biomarkers and AI in diagnosis, arguing that without patient participation, the effectiveness of precision approaches may be compromised. While the focus is on psychiatry, the underlying themes of patient engagement and the integration of AI in clinical settings could inform approaches in medical AI, particularly in developing interpretable models that prioritize clinician-patient collaboration. The insights on patient involvement may also resonate with efforts to enhance the clinical applicability of AI models in pathology.
reviewer_b_comment: While the paper is primarily situated in the field of psychiatry, its exploration of patient engagement and the critique of AI's role in clinical practice could provide valuable insights for the researcher's focus on interpretable AI in medical settings. The concepts of collaboration and therapeutic assessment may inspire similar approaches in pathology, particularly in ensuring that AI outputs are clinically meaningful and aligned with patient care.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, have achieved strong performance across multimodal tasks by aligning visual and textual representations in a shared embedding space. title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Forced Outage Risk Prediction: Benefits and Comparison to Machine Learning

abstract:

Abstract: This study examines the ability of large language models (LLMs) to predict the risk of weather-related forced outages in the distribution grid in a zero-shot framework, without labeled training data. authors: Adnan Anwar
abstract:
arXiv:2609.04943v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent benchmarks such as PowerGraph provide large collections of power-grid graphs for cascading-failure classification. Graph neural networks (GNNs) achieve strong predictive performance on this task, but typically require end-to-end training and model-specific tuning, while their latent representations can be difficult to relate to physically meaningful propagation patterns. title: Beyond Argmax: A Mechanistic Study of Semantic Retention in Frozen Foundation-Model Composition for Generalized Few-Shot 3D Segmentation
authors: Silas Kwabla Gah, Ebenezer Owusu
abstract:

Abstract: Classical classifier-combination work distinguishes score-level fusion from hard decision-level voting. We revisit this distinction where independently pretrained, frozen foundation models are composed at inference time for generalized few-shot 3D segmentation. We ask: how much useful semantic information is lost when heterogeneous sources are collapsed to a single class before they can interact?

Abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) systems, jointly interpreting images and natural language queries, hold significant promise across many domains, yet the privacy-sensitive nature of user data creates a fundamental barrier. abstract:

Abstract: Fine-grained robotic manipulation depends on understanding parts, not only whole objects. title: Judging by the Cover: Cleaning LLM Truthfulness Benchmarks to Avoid Surface-Level Feature Leakage

abstract:

Abstract: Binary-choice truth benchmarks ask models to choose between a correct and an incorrect answer, but if the two answers differ systematically in surface-level features, models can exceed chance without performing the intended reasoning. title: Safe Learning Under Irreversible Dynamics via Asking for Help
authors: Benjamin Plaut, Juan Li\'evano-Karim, Hanlin Zhu, Stuart Russell
abstract:
arXiv:2502.14043v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Most learning algorithms with formal regret guarantees essentially rely on trying all possible behaviors, which is problematic when some errors cannot be recovered from. Instead, we allow the learning agent to ask for help from a mentor and to transfer knowledge between similar states. We show that this combination enables the agent to learn both safely and effectively. Under standard online learning assumptions, we provide an algorithm whose regret and number of mentor queries are both sublinear in the time horizon for Markov decision processes with irreversible dynamics and infinite state spaces. title: Exploring Urban Land Use Patterns by Pattern Mining and Unsupervised Learning
authors: Zdena Dobesova, Tai Dinh, Pavel Novak
abstract:
arXiv:2604.13050v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Comparative planning needs reproducible methods for identifying recurring land-use configurations across cities. Using Urban Atlas 2018 data for 100 European urban areas, we construct 290,396 focal-neighborhood transactions and 1,543 frequent-itemset support features at 10\% minimum support. Ward clustering is applied in the original normalized feature space, with UMAP used only for visualization. A seven-cluster descriptive solution is retained through multi-criterion evaluation and 500 paired feature-subsampling repetitions. Sensitivity analyses show stable city-similarity geometry across 5--15\% thresholds but greater membership sensitivity to representation choices and non-artificial land-use content. The framework supports peer-city comparison while making scale and boundary limitations explicit.

title: Diffusion learning reveals viable parameter manifolds and compensation geometry in biological dynamical systems
authors: Ruilin Zhang, Louis Tao, Zhuo-Cheng Xiao
abstract:
arXiv:2607.03671v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Models of complex systems often have many parameters, yet are constrained by far fewer experimentally accessible observables; consequently, similar activity can emerge from coordinated parameter changes. We formalize these compatible parameter sets as \emph{viable parameter manifolds}: the inverse images of target dynamical features under a parameter-to-feature map. The relevant codimension is not the number of reported features, but the effective rank of that map at the target scale. Locally redundant features lower the effective codimension, while poor conditioning, high curvature, or regime mixing degrade learnability. title: From Information to Delegation: Mapping Human-AI Financial Decision Making
authors: Iman Munire Bilal, Yingcan Carol Wang, Ajan Raj, Filippo Giovagnini, Pranav Tewari, Yuwei Zhang, Mei-Chen Zoe Liou, Qamar Zaman
abstract:
arXiv:2608.02100v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As AI increasingly participates in human decision making, understanding how decision-making authority is distributed between humans and AI has become a fundamental behavioural question. We introduce a behavioural measurement framework combining intent and delegated decision authority to quantify what consumers seek from AI and how much decision-making authority they assign to it. Applied to 1.5 million real-world ChatGPT and Gemini interactions from 6,304 users in the United States and India, we find that financial services are already a substantial AI use case. Consumers overwhelmingly use AI to retrieve information and shape financial judgement, while delegation of financial execution remains rare. By shifting attention from conversation topics to delegated decision authority, this work establishes a behavioural baseline for measuring the transition to increasingly agentic AI.
